initial_observation.encounter_context: emergency room visit triggered by progression of symptoms
initial_observation.chief_complaint: progressive lower extremity numbness, pins and needles sensation, mild weakness, unstable gait
initial_observation.first_contact_summary: Two weeks prior to admission, she developed fever, cough and back pain and tested positive for COVID-19. Fever and cough resolved but back pain persisted. She then developed numbness and weakness in the lower extremities progressing to unstable gait, prompting emergency room visit. Physical exam showed stable vital signs, normal muscle strength and reflexes initially, admitted for idiopathic paresthesias with suspicion of lumbosacral radiculopathy.
presenting_symptoms: mild weakness in left lower extremity
known_prior_history: anterior cervical discectomy and anterior interbody arthrodesis at C4–C7 (3 years prior)

evidence_items.source_text: Two weeks prior to this hospital admission, she developed a fever, cough and back pain amidst the COVID-19 pandemic. The patient tested positive for COVID-19 and was treated with azithromycin for 5 days at home. Subsequently, over the next 2 weeks, her fever and cough resolved, but the lower back pain persisted. This was characterised by a throbbing, 7/10 intensity (numeric rating scale), radiating to both the lower extremities. She then had a new onset of numbness, pins and needles sensation in the left lower extremity associated with mild weakness. These same symptoms then progressed to the contralateral lower extremity over the next 24 hours with an unstable gait. This progression triggered an emergency room visit. She had no headaches, loss of consciousness, changes in mental status, changes in vision and speech, difficulty swallowing, seizure-like symptoms or urine/bowel incontinence.
evidence_items.temporal_cue: two weeks prior to hospital admission

evidence_items.source_text: Physical examination findings included stable vital signs and motor strength was 5/5 (Oxford Scale) in all four extremities, normal deep tendon reflexes in both upper and lower extremities and a negative Babinski sign bilaterally. There was no defined spine sensory level and no upper motor neuron weakness findings.

On the day of admission, notable laboratory findings include a white cell count of 13.5×109/L, normal erythrocyte sedimentation rate, C-reactive protein, vitamin B12 level andthyroid stimulating hormone.
The CT scan of the head showed no intraparenchymal mass or lesions, no haemorrhage and no findings of normal pressure hydrocephalus. Radiograph of the spine showed multilevel degenerative changes.

MRI of the lumbar spine without contrast (see figure 1) showed moderate bilateral and moderate left-sided neural foraminal narrowing at L2–L3 and L3–L4, respectively, and unremarkable conus medullaris.
Because of persistent headaches, an MRI of the brain was done, which showed normal findings.

Over the next 24 hours, a repeat COVID-19 test sent came back positive. The patient developed worsening weakness with muscle strength 3/5 in both lower extremities and new onset of weakness of her left upper extremity with muscle strength 4/5. Additional symptoms included numbness, tingling and paresthesias of the affected extremities. Now there was a change in her examination with diminished deep tendon reflexes when compared with the previous day.
CSF revealed findings suggestive of albumin-cytologic disassociation with a white cell count of 2 cu/mm and protein count of 117 mg/dL.

As the diagnosis of GBS became clearer, the patient was given 2 mg/kg intravenous immunoglobulins for 4 days and the respiratory status was monitored by checking vital capacity every 4 hours. She also received gabapentin 300 mg two times per day for neuropathic pain.
After receiving this treatment, the patient’s symptoms improved significantly and she was discharged to an acute rehabilitation facility for regular physical therapy.

hidden_reference.final_diagnosis_verbatim: With the patient exhibiting ascending weakness with diminished reflexes, an urgent lumbar puncture was performed to rule out GBS. Initially, a lumbar puncture was deferred as there was a low suspicion for GBS based on the patient’s presentation with normal deep tendon reflexes and an unremarkable conus medullaris. CSF revealed findings suggestive of albumin-cytologic disassociation with a white cell count of 2 cu/mm and protein count of 117 mg/dL.
diagnostic_reasoning_verbatim_spans: As the diagnosis of GBS became clearer, the patient was given 2 mg/kg intravenous immunoglobulins for 4 days and the respiratory status was monitored by checking vital capacity every 4 hours.
With the patient exhibiting ascending weakness with diminished reflexes, an urgent lumbar puncture was performed to rule out GBS.
Later as the patient exhibited clinical findings of ascending paralysis with diminished deep tendon reflexes, the diagnosis of GBS became more evident.
